Gottfried Leibniz. A German polymath from sixteen forty-six to seventeen sixteen: mathematician, philosopher, physicist, logician, and diplomat who independently developed calculus and created the notation still used today in every mathematics and physics classroom in the world.

Leibniz developed calculus independently of Newton, using infinitesimals and treating the quotient of differentials, dy over dx, as a true fraction that could be manipulated algebraically according to the rules of algebra. His notation—d for differential, the integral symbol—was so intuitive that it displaced Newton's fluxion notation by the eighteenth century and has never been replaced. He introduced the chain rule for derivatives and understood integration as the inverse of differentiation, founding the fundamental theorem of calculus. His approach proved superior for systematic development of the subject, which is why his notation and methods prevailed.

Beyond calculus, he pioneered symbolic logic. He attempted to create an ars combinatoria, a universal language for all knowledge using symbols and logical rules—a dream that would only be realised centuries later. He formulated the principle of indiscernibles: if two things have identical properties in every respect, they must be the same thing. His principle of sufficient reason asserts that every fact must have a reason or cause, an attempt to ground all of rational thought in logical necessity.

He developed the concept of monads—indivisible, immaterial units of reality that anticipated aspects of quantum mechanics centuries before quantum theory. He also contributed to the science of dynamics, exploring how force and motion relate, competing with Cartesian mechanics throughout his career. He believed the universe follows laws of perfect harmony.

Leibniz's mathematical notation won out decisively over all alternatives. Every physicist and engineer uses his integral symbol and d over dx notation today. His metaphysical system—monadology and pre-established harmony—was less influential, eventually superseded by Kant and later thinkers. Yet his dream of a symbolic logic, a universal language for reasoning, was realised two hundred years later in the twentieth century through formal logic and computer science. He stands as the last true Renaissance man: equally at home in mathematics, theology, diplomacy, and metaphysics, with contributions to each that shaped the future.
